transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in to see me?

Hello, doctor. I keep forgetting everyday things like appointments and errands, and it’s starting to really mess up taking care of my wife and my commitments in the garden project. I’ve just been feeling so scattered and overwhelmed trying to keep up with it all lately.
Did these memory and concentration problems start after a specific stressful life event or change, and have they been going on for less than 6 months?

I've always been a bit scattered, but it became a major issue after my wife had a stroke about 14 months ago and I had to take over her care and paperwork. So these difficulties have been going on for a little over a year now, which is definitely longer than six months.
Do you feel anxious or worried most days about many different things, and find it hard to control that worry even when there isn’t an immediate problem?
No, I wouldn't say I feel constantly anxious or worried in that way. It's more that I just feel incredibly overwhelmed and scattered trying to keep up with all of my daily tasks and responsibilities.
Since your wife’s stroke, have your symptoms caused clear trouble with your daily functioning, and did they start within about 3 months of that stressor?

Yes, they've caused real trouble—my wife has missed appointments, our bills and insurance forms are messed up, and I've had to step back from my garden and storytelling projects because people can't rely on me. It definitely started within a month or two of her stroke, right when I suddenly had to manage all of her care and paperwork.
Have your symptoms stayed mostly tied to the stress of your wife's stroke and caregiving, or have they continued to worsen even when things are calmer?

Honestly, these problems aren't really new; I've actually struggled with being easily distracted and restless my entire life, even back when I was a schoolboy. Having a loose schedule in retirement let me manage it, but now these issues persist even on calmer days because the baseline responsibilities of her care never truly go away.
Before your wife’s stroke and the recent caregiving stress, did you also have similar problems with inattention, forgetfulness, or restlessness starting in childhood or adolescence?

Yes, absolutely, it goes all the way back to childhood. Even in primary school, my teachers were always telling my parents that I couldn't sit still and was constantly talking out of turn. I'd also leave half-finished worksheets on my desk because I’d just lose track of what we were supposed to be doing.
Before age 12, did these attention problems also cause clear difficulties in more than one setting, such as at school and at home?

Yes, it definitely affected both. While school was the most obvious source of trouble with teachers constantly complaining that I couldn't sit still or finish my worksheets, it carried over to home because my parents were always being contacted about my behavior. They had to deal with that same restlessness and lack of focus at home, too.
Were your attention and restlessness problems present continuously since childhood, or did they mainly begin only after your wife's stroke and caregiving stress?

They have been there continuously since childhood, but I was always able to manage them with a loose, unstructured schedule. It was only after my wife's stroke 14 months ago, when I had to handle all of her care and paperwork, that these lifelong tendencies became a truly overwhelming problem.
Do you still have symptoms like fidgeting, feeling restless, interrupting others, or acting before thinking now, not just trouble with forgetfulness and concentration?

Yes, I absolutely still struggle with those things. I feel a constant jumpy energy in my body when I have to sit still, like in clinic waiting rooms, and I'm always on the move bouncing from one task to another. I also get very impatient and frequently interrupt people or blurt out answers before they've even finished speaking.

opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in to see me?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview confirms a lifelong pattern of inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity beginning in childhood, present in more than one setting (school and home), and persisting into adulthood with clear functional impairment. Symptoms include distractibility, forgetfulness, inability to finish tasks, restlessness, fidgety/jumpy energy, interrupting, and blurting out answers. Although caregiving stress worsened the impact, the core syndrome clearly predates the stressor, supporting ADHD, predominantly inattentive/combined presentation coded here as F90.0.
